Track 01 — Analytical tool
01IntroductionTeam 05 analytical tool

How much hotter can it get before each retrofit fails?

Heat Headroom gives every atrium retrofit one extra number: the degrees of further warming it can take before its overheating score passes 42 K·h.

Audience

MMU estates and the design team choosing an atrium retrofit meant to last decades.

Question

Which package stays below the overheating limit the longest, and what does that cost in daylight and openings?

Decision

Among the 1,041 designs that pass, pick one with headroom, not one that scrapes through.

17 June 2050, the hottest day of the hot week, one hour per step. One diamond per °C of atrium operative temperature; wavy diamonds are above 26 °C. EnergyPlus baseline and the 2050 weather file.

02Why · The problemProject context

Summer 2026 showed what overheating costs

Causes named in the brief: buildings designed for winter first, urban heat islands, and no overheating rules for the buildings we already have.

From the Heat Headroom study

2,877excess heat-associated deaths in England, May and June 2026
92%of UK buildings projected to overheat by 2050
0overheating rules for existing buildings

03Scope of studyAdaptive reuse

From the whole stock down to one atrium

Part O’s overheating rules cover new homes only. Existing buildings, and buildings converted to a new use, go unchecked. We study one of them closely enough to act on.

Adaptive reuse keeps adding homes with no overheating check

Homes made by converting offices, shops and other non-domestic buildings. The yearly number has fallen from about 30,000 to under 18,000, but every one of them sits outside Part O, and the stock they create keeps growing.

17,710homes from change of use, England, 2024–25
M15Geoffrey Manton’s postcode, high risk in Part O Appendix C

Gains from change of use, non-domestic to residential, England. gov.uk Housing supply: net additional dwellings (2015–16, 2017–18, 2018–19, 2021–22); 2024–25 from the Heat Headroom team plan. Years marked “no figure” are gaps in our checked data, not zeros.

05Our tool · How it works

The same sweep, repeated in a warmer world

  1. 01
    Warmer weatherShift the 2050 file by +0.5, +1 and +2 °C, the way FF Climate Morph does.
  2. 02
    Re-run EnergyPlus243 designs × 4 climates, about 1,000 runs of the official model.
  3. 03
    HeadroomThe extra warming each design takes before it passes 42 K·h, with its error measured.
  4. 04
    Show itColour the trade-off front by headroom. A “safe until” card for any design.

Bottom plane: real 2050 results for the 243-design grid. Upper planes are a placeholder until the warmer sweep runs.

06Our tool · Route map

The chain at a glance

The web app never opens a Rhino file. Geometry and results are written to JSON by Python scripts, the EnergyPlus sweep adds simulated results, and the browser reads only JSON. Each link in the chain can be rerun on its own.

Rhino 8

Exporters

JSON

Web app

The Grasshopper exporter also writes the files on the lower right. Only the two files feeding sweep_atrium.py change simulated scores; everything else changes what is shown or estimated.

Select any box to see what it reads, writes and how to rerun it.

    11SignificanceOpenness Analysis tool

    Why openness is the thing to analyse

    1. 01
      Evaluate the existing buildingScore the atrium as built before any proposal: 320.6 K·h, with 58 of 70 occupied hours above 26 °C.
    2. 02
      Locate weak pointsFind where the heat gets in. The atrium glass is 16% of the envelope but takes 28% of the hot-week sun.
    3. 03
      Cross-reference any proposalRun any design through the same model and benchmark it against the existing building on the same score, with its error.
    4. 04
      Openness is where the factors meetSolar gain, shading, day airflow, night purge and conduction all act through how open the envelope is, and they interact: the U-value effect even changes sign with shading.

    Lines per bundle are proportional to each lever’s spread: the range of the mean score across its five levels, over all 3,125 EnergyPlus runs. Roof screen 248 K·h, g-value 193, night ventilation 133, day ventilation 118, U-value 91.

    12Our tool · Trade-offs and honesty

    Every number labelled, every error measured

    A design with lots of headroom usually needs a heavy screen or very low g-value, which costs daylight, and big night vents. We plot headroom against daylight, vent opening and winter heat loss on one front.

    NumberWhere it comes fromHow wrong it might be
    Score, simulated designOfficial EnergyPlus modelOne well-mixed zone; real atria stratify
    Score, between designsInterpolation±4.8 K·h typical, 20.4 worst, measured
    HeadroomEnergyPlus at 4 climatesMeasured with our own off-grid runs
    Daylight, winter, ventsLabelled proxiesEditable assumptions; no glare, no wind
    Warmer climatesUniform shift of a crude morphFor comparing designs, not predicting years

    Context check: only 8 of the 99 neighbours within 150 m rise above the atrium clerestory (19.35 m). They cannot shade the roof in occupied hours.
